headline: Structural underinvestment in upstream oil and gas since 2015 crash supports higher-for-longer price outlook
reasoning: Kerr argues that oil and gas companies have persistently prioritised shareholder returns over new production since the 2015 oil crash, keeping global CapEx and drilling rig rates low for over a decade. Investors have treated energy as a sunset industry and demanded returns sooner rather than later, which has entrenched this capital discipline. Australian producers that bucked the trend and directed capital to growth were punished by investors, reinforcing the industry-wide behaviour. Kerr sees this as a key structural reason why prices will remain elevated as a supply deficit emerges even as demand for oil and gas products grows year on year.
quote: I think we've absolutely seen oil and gas companies prioritizing returns to shareholders, or over adding new production and new growth. The exception to this are being some of the Australian producers, and I think they've effectively been punished by investors for directing capital to growth, particularly during the Russia-Ukraine energy crisis in 2022. And we've really seen this behavior among the producers developed since the 2015 oil crash. So having to grow back over a decade now. And that's when we saw a global CapEx spend for upstream and drilling rig rates persistently remained low. And we just basically see this supply deficit emerge while we see a demand for oil and gas products increasing year on year.

headline: Mid-70s Brent likely represents a floor with a much higher potential ceiling given multi-decade low oil inventories
reasoning: Sarah Kerr notes oil started 2026 around $60/bbl before the Iran-Strait of Hormuz crisis pushed it to ~$120/bbl. Since the US-Iran 60-day MoU, Brent has fallen back to the mid-70s, which Kerr sees as a probable floor as the market prices in a return to normal within a month. However, she sees a meaningfully higher ceiling over coming quarters driven by multi-decade low oil inventory and reserve levels globally. The world has been drawing on reserves to bridge the supply crisis and cushion prices, and if Middle East supply does not resume before inventories run dry, prices could spike significantly higher.
quote: We think this is probably a likely floor because the market is effectively pricing in the world, returning to normal in one month's time in the future. But we see a much higher possible ceiling in the coming quarters, given, um, and that's just really driven by that, like multi-decade low oil inventory and reserve levels. So the world has effectively just been using its reserves to bridge the gap from this supply crisis to cushion oil prices. We see this reversing if supply from the Middle East doesn't resume before those inventory levels really just run dry.
